question: Recent confirmed cases of tuberculosis among farm workers from non-EU countries in West Achaea and Ilia in Greece prompted the health authorities to intervene, triggered epidemiological surveillance and brought to the fore serious concerns about the conditions faced by seasonal workers in terms of housing, hygiene and access to healthcare.

Similar cases have been recorded in other Member States, notably in Italy and Spain, suggesting that this is a Europe-wide issue. The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union enshrines human dignity, health protection and safe working conditions (Articles 1, 31 and 35).

Directive 2014/36/EU, in particular Articles 5, 20 and 23, provides for decent housing conditions and the equal treatment of seasonal workers. In addition, Directive 89/391/EEC and the European Pillar of Social Rights provide for a high level of health protection and safety for workers. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it have comparative data on the living conditions of seasonal farm workers in the Member States?
How does it assess the application of Directive 2014/36/EU to agricultural production sectors linked to common agricultural policy funding?
Does it intend to look into reinforced oversight mechanisms for the protection of public health and workers’ fundamental rights?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) The Commission is committed to ensuring dignified working and living conditions for thirdcountry seasonal workers. Directive 2014/36/EU1 provides specific requirements in this regard, including on adequate accommodation, equal treatment as regards working conditions and occupational safety and health, complaint mechanisms, redress and sanctions.

While public health surveillance, healthcare organisation and the enforcement of labour, housing and occupational safety and health rules are primarily the responsibility of Member States, the Commission monitors the correct implementation of Directive 2014/36/EU.

The Directive applies to third-country nationals admitted for seasonal work, including in agriculture, irrespective of whether the employer receives Common Agricultural Policy funding. The Commission has not harmonised EU-wide comparative data on seasonal farm workers’ living conditions. However, its 2026 implementation report on Directive 2014/36/EU2 confirmed that the Directive remains fit for purpose.
It identified persistent challenges in some Member States, notably on adequate accommodation, information provision, change of employer, complaints and redress, monitoring, inspections and sanctions.

As for the next steps, the Commission will continue monitoring the correct implementation of the Directive, including via the ongoing infringement procedures, and supporting Member States, including through Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund funding.

In the context of the upcoming Fair Labour Mobility Package, the planned revision of the European Labour Authority’s mandate aims, inter alia, to enable it to address abuses affecting third-country nationals, including seasonal workers.
1 Directive 2014/36/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on the conditions of

entry and stay of third-country nationals for the purpose of employment as seasonal workers, OJ L 94, 28.3.2014, pp. 375–390. 2 Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council in accordance with Article 27 of Directive 2014/36/EU on the conditions of entry and stay of third-country nationals for the purpose of employment as seasonal workers, 8.5.2026, COM(2026) 261 final.
